books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Election returns as published by the Library of Congress, Presidential Election of 1860: A Resource Guide (guides.loc.gov/presidential-election-1860), and the American Presidency Project (presidency.ucsb.edu/statistics/elections/1860). Popular-vote totals differ slightly between sources because of fusion tickets in New York and New Jersey.
stimulus.text:
Results of the presidential election of November 6, 1860. The Electoral College had 303 votes; 152 were needed to win.

| Candidate | Party | Popular votes | Share | Electoral votes |
| Abraham Lincoln | Republican | 1,865,908 | 39.8% | 180 |
| Stephen A. Douglas | Democratic | 1,380,202 | 29.5% | 12 |
| John C. Breckinridge | Southern Democratic | 848,019 | 18.1% | 72 |
| John Bell | Constitutional Union | 590,901 | 12.6% | 39 |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Which of the following is the best explanation for why Douglas, who won the second-most popular votes, won only 12 electoral votes?

options.text: His support was spread thinly across states he did not carry.
He won no votes in the Southern states.
options.misconception: Background: Douglas did win votes in the South, including Missouri, the one state he carried.

options.text: He was not on the ballot in the Northern states.
options.misconception: Background: Douglas was on the ballot across the North; he lost those states to Lincoln, he did not skip them.

options.text: His popular votes came mostly from non-voting territories.
options.misconception: Background: territories cast no electoral votes, and Douglas's votes came from the states, not the territories.

rationales.A: Electoral votes go to the winner of each state, so votes piled up in states a candidate loses buy nothing. Background: Douglas ran second in state after state in the North, so his large national total turned into almost no electoral votes.
rationales.B: Background: Douglas did win votes in the South, including Missouri, the one state he carried.
rationales.C: Background: Douglas was on the ballot across the North; he lost those states to Lincoln, he did not skip them.
rationales.D: Background: territories cast no electoral votes, and Douglas's votes came from the states, not the territories.
rationales.general:
1. The table shows the gap: 29.5 percent of the vote, but only 12 of 303 electors.
2. The Electoral College awards whole states, not a national total.
3. Background: Douglas finished second across the North, losing state after state to Lincoln by small margins.
4. Second place everywhere wins almost nothing.
Remember: in a winner-take-all state contest, where your votes sit matters more than how many you have.
